title: Private health insurers access patients' full medical records in 'aggressive' audits
full_text:
Private health insurers are potentially seeking too much access to patients' confidential medical information, through what has been described by the Australian Private Hospitals Association as "aggressive" audit practices.
Permission to access medical records is typically baked into the terms and privacy policy, which essentially grants the insurer permission to collect wide-ranging data on their customers — from security camera vision in their shopfronts, to personal social media posts.
Under agreements with patients and hospitals, insurers are entitled to ask a medical practitioner for a patient's notes relating to an episode of treatment, to ensure the correct procedure item numbers were billed.
But hospitals and allied health providers warn there have been cases of insurers asking providers for their patients' full clinical history.
It comes after ABC News reported concerns about claims of anti-competitive behaviour by health insurer Bupa and broader industry allegations of misuse of market power.
Insurers auditing allied health providers
One physiotherapist, who did not want to be identified for fear of retribution by insurers, told ABC News he had been subject to an aggressive audit twice by Bupa.
He said that during one audit, Bupa asked for the whole clinical history of his Bupa customers.
The physiotherapist wrote to his patients to seek their permission to release the documents and two-thirds refused.
When he told the insurer this, he said he received a letter stating the company wanted those details irrespective of patient consent and told him it was in his agreement with the insurer to be a preferred provider.
Industry experts told ABC News that when patients sign up to private health insurance, the terms of their insurance do allow for their records to be accessed during audits.
When the physio was told by the professional regulator, the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency, that he was not allowed to release the information because patients had not granted permission, he claims the insurer threatened him with having to repay up to $300,000 in benefits.
"If I went ahead and released those notes I could be struck from registration," he said.
It was not until he went to the Commonwealth Ombudsman that the situation was resolved.
"I rang a multitude of government agencies for help. I almost walked away from the industry," he said.
A Bupa spokesperson said the insurer does routine audits to make sure claims have been submitted and paid correctly, in line with any relevant agreements.
They said audits also ensure customers are paying the right amount of out-of-pocket gaps.
"These checks are done fairly and proportionately," they said.
The spokesperson said Bupa is committed to protecting customers' privacy and works constructively with providers to resolve issues.
"If there's a question about a claim, there are clear review and dispute processes in place, in line with consent, privacy and other legal requirements."
Dentists report insurer overreach
The Independent Dentist Network told ABC News dentists have reported health insurer overreach on their audits as well.
The network's managing director Merv Saultry noted a case of a large insurer before the pandemic that claimed a WA dentist had submitted $1 million in questionable claims.
He said the insurer sent in auditors, who the dentist claimed were unqualified to review his patient histories because they were dental practice managers or nurses, and not trained dentists.
They reported back to the insurer and wanted some treatments reclassified.
Negotiations and legal threats from the dentist saw the claim reduced to $500,000 and ultimately dropped with a warning.
"This case was bigger than most," he said.
Mr Saultry said the dentist was still traumatised by the case and also unwilling to speak publicly.
It is not the first time concerns about the qualifications of auditors and their ability to assess complex medical cases have been raised.
Bupa brought a Federal Court case against esteemed Sydney ophthalmologist Andrew Chang over a dispute on anaesthetics claims following an audit. Dr Chang declined to comment.
After a three-year legal battle that ended in 2019, Dr Chang won, and Bupa was ordered to pay his costs, with the judgement noting:
"It does not appear that an ophthalmologist peer with vitreoretinal subspecialist expertise has had input into BUPA's audit."
The private health insurance industry has previously said there was "tough behaviour" on both sides of industry negotiations, but the friction is needed to keep premiums down.
Releasing patient notes illegal: lawyer
The University of Sydney Law School's Bashi Hazard, who has studied the private health insurance industry, said it was illegal to release patient notes without their permission.
She said an insurer could not write terms into a contract that violated the law, and asking for patient notes outside an episode of care without their permission should void the contract.
"Whilst there's an obligation on a patient to disclose in order to get their insurance payouts, it still is very much a violation of the patient's rights if they haven't consented to that disclosure through the practitioner," Dr Hazard said.
"Patient confidentiality is a very, very serious obligation that we put on doctors and any healthcare provider.
"So the implications are quite significant for individual providers."
The Australian Private Hospitals Association chief executive Brett Heffernan said some hospitals had experienced similar pressure for entire clinical histories from insurers, describing it as "rogue behaviour".
"We're seeing more and more complaints from our members regarding aggressive audits," he said.
"What we're seeing increasingly from insurers now is they want the patient's full medical history.
"Now, that's not appropriate for hospitals to provide."
Mr Heffernan believed the conduct was illegal, and said hospitals have complained the audits have "a strong focus on minor technical compliance issues and punitive outcomes for deviations".
'Chaperones' to view records
The insurers are only allowed to look at a hospital medical record with a hospital chaperone.
The hospitals association said auditing was increasingly adding impost and cost to operations because they have to facilitate access.
"It is hard to believe patients are happy that [health] funds are trawling through their medical record and reviewing this," Mr Heffernan said.
The ABC understands the complex nature of overlapping health laws means the legality of some audits is less clear.
For example, prudential standards mean an insurer must ensure payment integrity and the terms of signing up to health insurance allow for auditing of any service they fund.
"If hospitals don't provide [the information], as they should not, the health funds are threatening penalties for obfuscation and trying to hide details, which they clearly are not," Mr Heffernan said.
"So it's another area where these contracts need to be cleaned up."
